title: Sampling and Experiments
description: Populations and samples, sampling distributions, sampling designs and their biases, and randomized experiments.
overview: Almost every data analysis tries to say something about more than the data in hand: all customers, not just those in the table; all future patients, not just those in the trial. The link between the data and the wider world is the way the data were collected. A random sample supports statements about the population it came from, with a known margin of error. A randomized experiment supports statements about cause and effect. Data collected by convenience support neither, however many rows there are.

This chapter develops the ideas that make inference possible: the distinction between a population and a sample, the sampling distribution of a statistic, the standard designs and their biases, and the logic of randomized experiments and A/B tests. It is the base for the next chapters on estimation and hypothesis testing.
objectives: Distinguish population, sample, parameter and statistic, and describe the sampling distribution of the sample mean.
Compare simple random, stratified, cluster and convenience samples, and identify selection, non-response and survivorship bias.
Compute the margin of error of a proportion and the sample size needed for a target margin.
Explain why randomization supports causal conclusions, and design a randomized experiment or A/B test with control, blinding and blocking.
Recognize how sampling bias appears in machine learning data and evaluation.

sections.title: Populations, samples and sampling distributions
body: To judge a pot of soup, you taste one spoonful. The spoonful is the sample, and the pot is the population. If the soup is well stirred, the spoonful tells you about the pot. If you only ever taste the top, where the salt has not mixed in, you will be misled however large the spoonful. How the sample is taken matters more than how big it is. The **population** is the entire group we want to learn about (all adult residents of a country, all transactions of next year). A **parameter** is a numerical feature of the population: its mean μ, a proportion p. We seldom observe the whole population, so we study a **sample**, a subset, and compute a **statistic** (the sample mean x̄, the sample proportion p̂) as an estimate of the parameter.

A **simple random sample** (SRS) of size n gives every possible subset of size n the same chance of being chosen. Different samples give different statistics, so the statistic is itself a random variable. Its distribution over repeated samples is the **sampling distribution**, which describes how much an estimate varies from sample to sample, and so how far it is likely to be from the truth.

example.title: A sampling distribution, exactly
example.problem: A population has four values, 2, 4, 6, 8 (mean 5, variance 5). List the sample means of all 16 samples of size 2 drawn with replacement, and compute their mean and variance.
solution: The mean of the sample means is (2 + 6 + 12 + 20 + 18 + 14 + 8)/16 = 5: the sample mean is **unbiased** for μ. Their variance is [9 + 2(4) + 3(1) + 0 + 3(1) + 2(4) + 9]/16 = 40/16 = 2.5 = σ²/n = 5/2. The distribution of the sample mean is also more concentrated and more bell-shaped than the population, as the central limit theorem predicts.

body.key: For independent draws, the sample mean has mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n. This standard deviation of a statistic is its **standard error**: it shrinks with the square root of the sample size. To halve the error, quadruple the sample (see Limit Theorems).

list: The standard error says how much the //statistic// varies; the standard deviation σ says how much the //data// vary. Confusing them is a common mistake.

When sampling a sizable fraction N_s/N_pop of a finite population without replacement, the standard error is reduced by the **finite population correction** √(1 − n/N). It matters only when the sample is more than a few percent of the population. Beyond that, the precision depends on the absolute sample size, not on the fraction of the population: a sample of 1000 estimates a proportion about as well for a city of 100,000 as for a country of 100 million.
The sample proportion p̂ has standard error √(p(1 − p)/n).

body: A random error shrinks as n grows. A **bias** (systematic error) does not: a million biased observations are a million wrong answers. The common sources:

list: **Selection bias**: the sampling procedure favors some members of the population. The sampling frame may omit people (a phone survey misses people without phones).
**Non-response bias**: the people who respond differ from those who do not.
**Voluntary response bias**: self-selected respondents are typically those with strong opinions.

**Survivorship bias**: only the units that 'survived' some filter are observed. Studying successful companies to find the secrets of success ignores the failed ones with the same practices; in the Second World War, armor was proposed for the places where returned bombers had bullet holes, until Abraham Wald pointed out that the planes hit elsewhere never came back.
**Measurement bias**: leading or sensitive questions, instrument error, social desirability.

example.title: Size is no defense against bias
example.problem: In 1936 the Literary Digest magazine mailed 10 million questionnaires to people from telephone directories and club lists, and 2.4 million replied, predicting a landslide for Alf Landon over Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with 61% of the vote. George Gallup predicted Roosevelt using about 50,000 people. Why was the huge poll wrong?
example.solution: The frame (telephone and club members, in the Depression) over-represented wealthier voters, who favored Landon, and the voluntary response added non-response bias. The size reduced the random error to nearly zero while leaving the bias untouched. Gallup's smaller quota-based sample was chosen to resemble the electorate. The lesson: a biased sample is a precisely wrong answer.

example.title: Sample size for a poll
example.problem: How large must a random sample be for a margin of error of 3 percentage points, and of 1 point?
example.solution: n ≈ 0.96/0.03² = 1067 for ±3%, and 0.96/0.01² = 9604 for ±1%. Cutting the margin to a third costs nine times as many respondents. With n = 1000 the margin is 0.98/√1000 = 3.1%. This applies to simple random samples only; clustering enlarges the error by the **design effect** 1 + (m − 1)ρ for clusters of size m with intra-cluster correlation ρ (for m = 20 and ρ = 0.05: 1.95, so the effective sample size is about half the nominal one).

body: When the sample under-represents some groups, **weights** correct for it: each respondent counts in proportion to the number of population members they represent. Weighting fixes known imbalances in observed variables but cannot repair bias caused by unobserved ones.

sections.title: Randomized experiments
body: Suppose people who take vitamins are healthier than people who do not. Did the vitamins help, or do people who take vitamins also tend to exercise and eat well? Random assignment settles it: if a coin flip decides who gets the vitamin, the two groups will be alike in everything else on average, so any remaining difference in health can be credited to the vitamin. That is why randomized experiments are the strongest evidence for cause and effect. To learn the effect of a treatment (a drug, a price, a web page design), compare outcomes of units that received it with those that did not. In an **observational study** the units choose or are assigned treatments by some process outside the investigator's control, and the groups usually differ in other ways, so the comparison is **confounded** (see Simpson's paradox). People who take vitamins are healthier for many reasons other than the vitamins.

body.key: In a **randomized controlled trial**, the investigator assigns units to treatment or control by a random mechanism (a coin flip, a random number). Randomization makes the groups comparable on average in every respect, those that are measured and those that are not, so any systematic difference in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.

body: Why this works: assignment is independent of every pre-treatment characteristic, including the unmeasured ones. With 8 patients and 4 to be treated, there are C(8, 4) = 70 equally likely assignments. Whatever the (unknown) health of each patient, the chance that treated and untreated groups differ in average health is symmetric around zero, and the difference shrinks as the groups grow. The only systematic difference left between the groups is the treatment.

list: **Control group**: the comparison group, receiving no treatment, the standard treatment or a **placebo** (an inert treatment), which separates the effect of the treatment from the effect of expecting to be treated.

**Blinding**: in a **single-blind** study subjects do not know their group; in a **double-blind** study neither do the people who deliver the treatment or evaluate the outcome, preventing expectations from biasing the results.
**Replication**: enough units, and repeated studies, for the effect to stand out from chance.

**Blocking**: first group units by a variable known to affect the outcome (age group, site), then randomize within each block. It balances that variable exactly and increases precision (like stratified sampling).
**Randomize the unit that is treated**: if treatment is delivered to classrooms, randomize classrooms, not students; the analysis must follow the design.

body: An **A/B test** is a randomized experiment in a product: visitors are randomly assigned to the current version A or a variant B and a metric (conversion, revenue, retention) is compared. Randomization at the user level makes the comparison causal.

list: Decide the **hypothesis, the primary metric, the sample size and the stopping rule in advance** (see Hypothesis Testing for the power calculation). Peeking at the results every day and stopping when they look significant inflates false positives.
Check that the assignment worked: the two groups should have similar sizes (a **sample-ratio mismatch** signals a bug) and similar pre-experiment characteristics.
**Interference**: if one unit's treatment affects another's outcome (a social network, a marketplace where buyers compete), the simple comparison is biased. Randomize clusters or use other designs.
**Novelty and seasonality effects**: run long enough to see steady behavior, over whole weeks.
**Ethics**: experiments on people need consent or a justified waiver, minimal harm, and review.

body: A well-run randomized experiment has high **internal validity**: the estimated effect is the true effect for the participants in the study. Whether it applies to other people, places or times is **external validity**, which depends on how the participants were selected and on whether the setting resembles the target. A drug trial on healthy young volunteers may say little about elderly patients with other conditions.

body.note: When experiments are impossible or unethical (smoking and cancer, the effect of a policy on a country), causal conclusions must come from observational data and extra assumptions, or from natural experiments in which nature or a rule assigns treatment as if at random (see Causal Inference).

sections.title: Sampling bias in machine learning
body: Machine learning data sets are samples too, and the same questions apply: from what population were the examples drawn, and is that the population on which the model will be used?

list: **Selection in the labels**: a loan model trained on past decisions sees outcomes (repayment) only for applicants who were approved. A medical model trained on patients who were tested sees labels only for them. The model learns about the selected population, and extrapolates to the rest without any evidence.

**Convenience data**: images scraped from the web over-represent some countries, languages and demographics. A face recognition model trained mostly on light-skinned faces performs worse on dark-skinned ones; a speech model trained on one accent fails on others.

**Dataset shift**: the data seen after deployment differ from the training data because of time (covariate shift: the distribution of inputs changes), a change in the relationship between inputs and outputs (concept drift) or a change in the population. Monitor inputs and performance after deployment.
**Feedback loops**: a model's decisions shape the data it will later be retrained on (a recommender only sees clicks on what it showed). The data are then no longer a sample of the world.

**Evaluation samples**: the test set must be drawn from the deployment distribution, with the splits made by the unit that matters (by patient, by user, by time: not by random row), or the reported accuracy is optimistic (see Generalization).

example.title: Correcting a covariate shift by weighting
example.problem: A model is trained on data in which 80% of the examples come from group A and 20% from group B, but in deployment the groups are 50% and 50%. How should the training examples be weighted to match deployment?
example.solution: Use importance weights w = (deployment share)/(training share): 0.5/0.8 = 0.625 for each group A example and 0.5/0.2 = 2.5 for each group B example. Weighting the loss this way makes the training objective equal in expectation to the deployment objective, provided the relationship between inputs and labels is the same in both populations. Large weights make estimates noisy, and the correction cannot make up for groups that are missing from the training data.

body: **Active learning** chooses which examples to label next (the uncertain ones), which makes the labeled set a deliberately biased sample that is very informative, and so requires care when estimating accuracy on it. **Stratified splits** keep class proportions the same across train and test sets, which is important for rare classes (see Evaluating Models).

quiz.q: A random sample of 400 voters finds that 20% support a measure. What is the standard error of the sample proportion?
quiz.why: SE = √(p(1 − p)/n) = √(0.2 × 0.8/400) = √0.0004 = 0.02. Forgetting the square root gives 0.0004, and 0.04 is the margin of error (about 2 SE).

quiz.q: The standard error of a sample mean is 8 when n = 50. What sample size gives a standard error of 2?
quiz.why: The standard error is proportional to 1/√n. Dividing it by 4 requires multiplying n by 4² = 16, and 50 × 16 = 800.

quiz.q: A population consists of the four values 1, 2, 3 and 6, with variance 3.5. Samples of size 2 are drawn with replacement. What is the variance of the sample mean?
quiz.why: For independent draws the variance of the sample mean is σ²/n = 3.5/2 = 1.75. The variance of the data, 3.5, describes individual values, not means.

quiz.q: A poll takes 1000 random respondents from a town of 50,000 and another poll takes 1000 from a country of 50 million. Both populations have the same variance. How do the precisions compare?
quiz.a: They are almost identical, since precision depends on the absolute sample size
wrong: The town poll is far more precise because it covers a larger fraction of its population
The country poll is far more precise because its population is larger
The town poll is exactly twice as precise as the country poll
quiz.why: The finite population correction is √(1 − 1000/50,000) ≈ 0.99 for the town and about 1 for the country. Unless the sample is a sizable share of the population, only n matters.

quiz.q: Researchers randomly choose 10 villages and survey every household in each. What is this design, and what is its main drawback?
quiz.a: A cluster sample, which is less precise than a random sample of equal size
wrong: A stratified sample, whose main drawback is that stratum sizes must be known beforehand
A systematic sample, whose main drawback is alignment with a periodic pattern in the list
A convenience sample, whose main drawback is that its error cannot be bounded at all
quiz.why: Sampling whole groups is cheap, but households in one village are similar, so each adds less new information than an independent draw. The effect is measured by the design effect.

quiz.q: An analysis of mutual funds that exist today reports a high average return over the past 20 years. What is a major flaw?
quiz.a: Survivorship bias: funds that did badly and closed are missing
wrong: Non-response bias: some funds refused to report their returns to the researchers
Measurement bias: returns are reported in percent instead of in dollars
Voluntary response: investors chose which funds would be included in the data
quiz.why: Only units that survived a filter are observed, so the sample is skewed toward successes. The failed funds had the same strategies but are absent from the data.

quiz.q: What sample size does a simple random sample need for a worst-case 95% margin of error of about 2 percentage points?
wrong: About 1,200
About 4,800
About 9,600
quiz.why: n ≈ 0.96/ME² = 0.96/0.02² = 2400. Halving the margin from 4 points would need four times the sample, and ±1 point needs 9,600.

quiz.q: A survey of 1900 respondents uses clusters of m = 10, with intra-cluster correlation ρ = 0.1. What is the approximate effective sample size?
quiz.why: The design effect is 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + 9 × 0.1 = 1.9. The effective sample size is 1900/1.9 = 1000, so clustering costs almost half the information.

quiz.q: An interviewer records sales on every 7th day, starting from a Monday, in a shop with a strong weekly cycle. What is the weakness of this systematic sample?
quiz.a: The interval matches the weekly cycle, so every sampled day is a Monday
wrong: Days far apart in time resemble each other too much to add information
Systematic samples cannot be applied to data that are indexed by dates
Each day has equal probability, so the sample is unbiased but expensive to collect
quiz.why: Taking every k-th unit can line up with a periodic pattern in the list, producing a sample that is not representative of the full cycle.

quiz.q: Six patients are to be split at random into a treatment group of 3 and a control group of 3. How many equally likely assignments are there?
quiz.why: The number of ways to choose which 3 of 6 are treated is C(6, 3) = 20. Randomization picks one of them with equal probability, which is what balances the groups on average.

quiz.q: A trial is run in three hospitals whose patients differ in severity. Patients are randomized to treatment or control separately within each hospital. What is this design called, and what does it achieve?
quiz.a: Blocking; it balances hospital exactly and improves precision
wrong: Blinding; it keeps patients from knowing their group
Cluster sampling; it randomizes whole hospitals to a treatment
Replication; it repeats the trial until the effect is significant
quiz.why: Grouping units by a variable known to affect the outcome and randomizing within the groups removes that variable from the comparison, as stratification does for samples.

quiz.q: An A/B test is planned as a 50/50 split of visitors. After a day, 12,000 visitors have seen version A and 8,000 version B. What does this suggest?
quiz.a: A sample-ratio mismatch, which points to a bug in the assignment
wrong: Normal random variation, since group sizes never match exactly
That version B is less appealing, since fewer people chose it
That the test has high power, because one group is larger
quiz.why: Assignment is random and does not depend on the visitor's response, so the group sizes should be close to equal. A large imbalance means the assignment or logging is broken and the results cannot be trusted.

quiz.q: A team checks an A/B test every morning and stops it the first day the p-value drops below 0.05. What is the problem?
quiz.a: Repeated peeking inflates the false-positive rate
wrong: Stopping early always lowers the power of the test to exactly zero
P-values cannot be computed before the planned end date of the test
It makes the two groups unequal in size by the end of the test
quiz.why: Every look is another chance to see a spurious significant result. The sample size and stopping rule should be fixed before the test starts.

quiz.q: A randomized test of a checkout design in the US in December shows a clear lift. The company plans to roll it out in Japan in July. What is the main concern?
quiz.a: External validity: the effect may not carry over to another population and season
wrong: Internal validity: randomization cannot show a causal effect in the first place
Blinding: users must not be told which design they have been shown
Selection bias: the US visitors chose which design they wanted to see
quiz.why: Randomization secures a causal estimate for the participants in the study. Whether it transfers to other people, places or times depends on how similar the setting is.

quiz.q: A model is trained with 90% of the examples from group A and 10% from group B, but deployment is 60% A and 40% B. What importance weight should each group B example get?
quiz.why: The weight is the deployment share divided by the training share: 0.4/0.1 = 4. Group A examples get 0.6/0.9 = 0.67.

quiz.q: A recommender is retrained every week on the clicks it received. Why does this threaten the quality of its data?
quiz.a: It only sees outcomes for items it chose to show
wrong: Clicks are measured with too much random error to be useful
The training set grows too large to fit in memory
Items that were shown can no longer be clicked again
quiz.why: The model's own decisions determine which outcomes are observed. This feedback loop makes the retraining data a biased reflection of the model's past behavior.

quiz.q: A model predicts outcomes per patient, and each patient has several visits in the data. The rows are split into training and test sets at random. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: The same patient appears in both sets, so the reported accuracy is optimistic
wrong: The classes become imbalanced in the training set
The test set becomes too small to compute any accuracy
The training labels are no longer random
quiz.why: The test set must mimic the deployment case of new patients. Splitting by patient keeps all visits of a person on one side.

quiz.q: A fraud model's input features have the same distribution as before, but fraudsters have changed their methods, so the same inputs now indicate fraud with a different probability. What is this?
quiz.a: Concept drift, a change in the relationship between inputs and outputs
wrong: Covariate shift, a change in the distribution of the inputs
Survivorship bias, since failed attempts are not observed
Voluntary response bias, since fraudsters report themselves
quiz.why: Covariate shift changes how often inputs occur, while concept drift changes what the inputs mean for the label. The first can be reweighted, but the second requires retraining on new data.

summary: Parameters describe a population, and statistics are computed from a sample. The sampling distribution of a statistic shows its variability; the standard error of a mean is σ/√n, of a proportion √(p(1 − p)/n). Precision depends on the sample size, not on the fraction of the population.

Random sampling (simple, stratified, cluster) supports inference. Convenience and voluntary samples have unknown bias. Bias does not shrink with n: a huge biased sample is precisely wrong (Literary Digest 1936).
The margin of error for a proportion is about 0.98/√n at 95%: n ≈ 1070 for ±3%, 9600 for ±1%. Cluster sampling has a design effect 1 + (m − 1)ρ.

Randomized controlled experiments make groups comparable on average in all characteristics, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment. Use control, placebo, blinding, blocking, a pre-specified plan, and watch for interference. Internal validity is not external validity.
ML data have selection, shift and feedback problems; evaluate on data that match the deployment population, split by the right unit, and use weights or monitoring where they differ.

problems.q: A population of 10,000 has σ = 15. Find the standard error of the mean of a simple random sample of n = 225, and the sample size needed to make it 0.5.
A poll of 1600 people finds 54% support a measure. Give the margin of error and a 95% interval, and say whether a majority is clearly supported.
problems.solution: SE = √(0.54 × 0.46/1600) = 0.01246, so ME = 1.96 × 0.01246 = 0.0244. The interval is 54% ± 2.4%, i.e. (51.6%, 56.4%), entirely above 50%, so the sample supports a majority (assuming a random sample and no non-response bias).

problems.q: A region is 60% urban and 40% rural. A stratified random sample of 500 people is taken, proportional to the population. How many from each stratum?
An online review site shows an average of 4.6 stars from 200 voluntary reviews. List two reasons why this may not represent all customers.
problems.solution: Voluntary response: people with very good or very bad experiences are more likely to review; non-reviewers (the majority) are unrepresented. Also, reviews can be incentivized, fake or removed, and only customers who completed a purchase (survivors) can review.
problems.a: Self-selection toward extreme experiences, and non-response from the silent majority (also incentives and survivorship).

problems.q: A new web page is tested on 5000 visitors in each group. Visitors were assigned by whether they arrived before or after noon. Why is this not a valid experiment, and how should it be assigned?
problems.solution: Time of day is confounded with the treatment: people browsing in the morning differ from those in the afternoon, so any difference could reflect who the visitors are. Assign visitors at random (for example, by hashing the user id or by a random draw on arrival), so that both versions run at the same time on comparable visitors.
problems.a: Assignment by time confounds treatment with visitor type; assign at random, concurrently.
